evidence: Plaut. Persa 114–115: id tōtum prōcēdit diem
Quint. 6.3.9: tōtum corpus vī suā concutit
terms.comment: With a word of time the accusative alone means “all … long” (tōtum diem); with other nouns Latin uses per: per tōtum iter, the whole way.

terms.gloss: whole, all together; as a whole
evidence: Tac. Agr. 12.2: singulī pugnant, ūniversī vincuntur
Tac. Germ. 5.1: in ūniversum, “on the whole”

terms.gloss: all, every; the whole of (a thing taken as one)
evidence: Caes. BG 1.1.1: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs

terms.comment: Mostly in the plural: cūnctī, all of them together.

phrases.latin: Māne quod tū occēperis negōtium agere, id tōtum prōcēdit diem.
phrases.english: Whatever business you start in the morning goes well the whole day.

phrases.latin: quoūsque calceī nusquam, toga fēriāta, līber tōtus diēs?
phrases.english: how long will it be no shoes, the toga on holiday, the whole day free?

phrases.latin: jānua nē versō strīdōrēs cardine reddat, nūlla domō tōtā est
phrases.english: so that no door may creak on its turning hinge, there is not one in the whole house

sources: Lewis & Short: totus · Lewis & Short: universus · Lewis & Short: omnis · Lewis & Short: cunctus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 407.
